claims.claim: The Newcomen engine condensed steam by injecting a spray of cold water directly into the working cylinder, creating the vacuum for the power stroke.
claims.episode_span: The cylinder was deliberately flooded with cold water to condense the steam, then the same metal mass had to be reheated with fresh steam before the next cycle could begin.
claims.supporting_quote: The regulator valve was then closed and the water injection valve V' briefly snapped open and shut, sending a spray of cold water into the cylinder. This condensed the steam and created a partial vacuum under the piston

claims.claim: The Newcomen design's dominant loss was that the cooled cylinder walls condensed fresh steam on every stroke, so a large share of the fuel went to reheating the same metal.
claims.episode_span: Most of the heat therefore never produced mechanical work; it cycled endlessly between the boiler and the cylinder walls.
claims.supporting_quote: After the water vapor within was cooled enough to create the vacuum, the cylinder walls were cold enough to condense some of the steam as it was admitted during the next intake stroke

claims.claim: Watt moved condensation into a separate external condenser vessel connected to the cylinder by a pipe, so the working cylinder could stay hot.
claims.episode_span: moved the condensation step to a separate vessel kept cold while the working cylinder stayed hot
claims.supporting_quote: In the Watt steam engine , condensation took place in an exterior condenser unit, attached to the steam cylinder via a pipe

claims.claim: Watt surrounded the cylinder with a steam jacket to keep it warm and prevent condensation within it.
claims.episode_span: Watt also added a steam jacket around the cylinder to reduce heat loss to the surroundings
claims.supporting_quote: surround the cylinder with a jacket. Steam was passed through the jacket before being admitted below the piston, keeping the piston and cylinder warm to prevent condensation within it

claims.claim: Watt's engine burned a small fraction of the fuel of a comparable Newcomen engine: sources report figures from about half (early commercial design) to about a quarter (fully developed), a range that brackets the digest's 'roughly one-third'.
claims.episode_span: Watt’s engine reduced fuel consumption to roughly one-third that of a comparable Newcomen engine under similar lift conditions
claims.supporting_quote: As fully developed, it used about 75% less fuel than a similar Newcomen one

claims.claim: Watt built his separate-condenser model in Glasgow in 1765; Newcomen engines wasted fuel because their cycle continually heated and cooled the cylinder, and the separate condenser let the cylinder stay hot, greatly increasing fuel efficiency.
claims.episode_span: Watt therefore asked what would happen if condensation occurred in a vessel that never shared temperature with the working cylinder. The separate condenser kept the cylinder near the temperature of incoming steam while the condenser itself remained cool enough to collapse the steam rapidly.
claims.source_title: Watt's second separate condenser, 1765. | Science Museum Group Collection
claims.supporting_quote: Early Newcomen engines were inefficient as their working cycle entailed continual heating and cooling of the cylinder, which wasted fuel. The separate condenser meant the steam was condensed in a separate chamber, allowing the cylinder to be kept hot and greatly increasing fuel efficiency.

claims.claim: Watt's separate-condenser patent was granted on 5 January 1769 ('A new method of lessening the consumption of steam and fuel in fire-engines'); engines with the condenser burned about two-thirds less coal, which let steam power move off the coalfields into factories and mills.
claims.episode_span: The new design could therefore be installed at factories and mills distant from coal supplies, expanding the market for steam power beyond the pithead.
claims.source_title: James Watt and the separate condenser - Science Museum Blog
claims.supporting_quote: Steam engines with Watt’s condenser burned 2/3rds less coal, making them capable of working not just on mines but in factories, mills, workshops, and anywhere else that needed power.

claims.claim: The first Newcomen engines converted only about a third of one percent of their fuel energy into work; Watt's improved engines were roughly fifteen times as efficient (i.e. a few percent).
claims.episode_span: engines converted well under one percent of their fuel's energy into work
claims.source_title: Yet Another Energy Crisis | The Engines of Our Ingenuity (University of Houston)
claims.supporting_quote: The first Newcomen engines had efficiencies around a third of one percent. By the time James Watt had finished his improvements, steam engines were fifteen times as efficient.

claims.claim: The Newcomen engine was staggeringly inefficient and burned vast quantities of coal, yet succeeded commercially for a time because it was the only practical alternative to horse-powered mine pumps.
claims.episode_span: Away from the mines the same engine could not compete with horses or water wheels because the fuel bill quickly exceeded any labor savings.
claims.source_title: Thomas Newcomen and the Steam Engine - Engineering and Technology History Wiki
claims.supporting_quote: The Newcomen engine was staggeringly inefficient by today's standards, but it was a commercial success for a time because it was the only practical alternative to pumps powered by horses.
